input.description: Research series cardinality limits in comparable systems
input.prompt:
Research task (not code, not jigc actions — just investigate and report back).

Context: I'm about to write a jigc `research` doc (slots: question, findings, sources) about a design gap in this repo's `MemoryStore` (src/store.ts): it's a `Map<string, Sample[]>` keyed by series name, with `maxSamples` bounding samples *per series*, but nothing bounds the number of distinct series (map keys). A single runaway label (e.g. a series name derived from unbounded user input, or a UUID/timestamp accidentally embedded in a series name) grows the map unboundedly and can OOM the process. This is the classic "cardinality explosion" problem in time-series/metrics systems.

Do web research (use WebSearch/WebFetch) on how comparable real-world systems handle unbounded label/series cardinality, and what it costs them operationally. I want concrete, citable specifics — not generic "cardinality is bad" content. Cover at least:

1. **Prometheus** — `sample_limit` in scrape configs, any series/label limits, and the well-documented OOM failure mode from cardinality explosions. What's the actual mechanism (reject whole scrape vs. drop samples) and its cost/tradeoff?
2. **Cortex/Mimir (Grafana)** — per-tenant active series limits (e.g. `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` or Mimir's equivalent), what happens when the limit is hit (429s to the client?), and what that costs (dropped writes, tenant needs to request limit increase, etc).
3. **VictoriaMetrics** — `-storage.maxHourlySeries` / `-storage.maxDailySeries` flags, what they do when hit, and the tradeoff.
4. **InfluxDB** — the classic "series cardinality" failure mode (in-memory index per series), any `max-series-per-database` / `max-values-per-tag` limits in 1.x, and what happens when hit.
5. **Datadog or another SaaS metrics vendor** — cardinality-based billing / "custom metrics" limits as a *cost-based* rather than technical bound (e.g. Datadog's "Metrics without Limits").

For each, note: (a) the actual bounding mechanism, (b) what happens to the write/series that exceeds it (reject new series? evict old? drop samples? bill more?), (c) what it costs operationally or financially, (d) a real citable source (official docs, engineering blog, or well-known incident writeup) with URL.

Also note the general design-pattern takeaway across these systems: is there a common shape to how they bound cardinality (e.g., a hard cap on distinct series count, enforced at write time, with new series beyond the cap rejected while existing ones keep flowing — as opposed to LRU-evicting old series to make room)?

Report back in plain text (no file writes, no jigc calls) as:
- A "findings" section: 4-6 tight paragraphs I can adapt almost verbatim into the research doc's findings slot — concrete, specific, with mechanism/cost per system, then the cross-system takeaway.
- A "sources" section: a plain list of `[Title](URL) — one-line note on what it supports`, one per source actually used.

Keep total findings prose to roughly 400-600 words — dense and specific, not padded.

input.description: Check jigc doc author payload grammar

content.content:
Author a whole instance from one declarative payload — the batch verb.

The doctype-general batch write: applies the equivalent `create` plus N
`add-item` / `set-slot` / `set-field` over a single buffer, persisting once.
In the payload, a slot value is a YAML block scalar wrapped in literal
`<<…>>` markers (`summary: |` then, indented beneath it, `<<the prose>>`) —
required syntax that tags the value as slot prose, not a fill-me
placeholder to delete; the block scalar keeps multi-paragraph and bulleted
prose intact where a quoted flow scalar would fold the line breaks. An
inline field takes a bare value (wrapping one is rejected).

Reach for `author` to write a whole instance in one shot (a migration, or any
many-leaf doc) — it collapses what would be a `create` + N follow-up calls.
Use `create` then `set-slot`/`set-field`/`add-item` for incremental,
one-leaf-at-a-time authoring instead. Run `author` instead of those verbs, or
after them — the create `author` implies over a doc this task already staged
acks `already existed — copied in for update` and changes nothing.

Over a COMMITTED doc `author` copies the committed body in as the edit base
and writes three ways: a payload item the doc does not hold is **appended**
(the committed items stay untouched); an existing doc-level leaf you
re-author overwrites **in place**; and a payload item whose title mints an id
the doc ALREADY holds is refused (`write.already-present`) with the whole
payload rejected and nothing staged — edit that item in place with
`set-slot`/`set-field` instead of re-authoring it here.

The fourth thing it does NOT do is rewrite the doc's title. The payload's
`title:` is the create id-source; over a doc this task already holds (or a
committed one copied in) the `# H1` stays as it is, so a `title:` that would be
silently dropped is refused (`write.title-ignored`) — as is a singleton's, whose
`# H1` is the schema's own `display-title`. A `title:` that mints a DIFFERENT id
is refused too (`write.identity-change`): that is a second document, not a
correction. Both reject the whole payload with nothing staged, and both route at
`jigc doc rename`, the in-task title change.

Payload shape (YAML; `--from-file`), mirroring the document's structure:

```yaml
    title: <the create id-source>
    sections:
      - id: <section-id>
        set:                    # doc-level leaves: fields + slots
          status: accepted      # inline field — a bare value
          summary: |
            <<the slot prose>>   # slot — <<…>>-wrapped block scalar
        items:                  # repeatable rows under this section
          - title: <item id-source>
            set:
              date: 2026-07-11
            sections:           # nested repeatable level, parented by the item
              - id: <nested-section-id>
                set: { note: <<inline slot>> }
      - id: <section-id>        # a section that IS one slot (a simple section):
        set: {<section-id>: <<…>>}   # its own slot, keyed by the section's own id
```

Usage: jigc doc author [OPTIONS] --from-file <FROM_FILE> <DOCTYPE>

Arguments:
  <DOCTYPE>
          The doctype to author (e.g. `changelog`) — minted through the create-gate

Options:
      --format <FORMAT>
          Output format: `agent` (default, terse text for a coding agent) · `json` (machine-readable) · `human` (formatted for a terminal)
          
          [default: agent]
          [possible values: agent, json, human]

      --from-file <FROM_FILE>
          The payload source: a path, or `-` for stdin (the whole-doc payload is large, so it arrives the same way slot prose does — never inline)

      --task <TASK>
          The active task to scope the write to. Optional: explicit wins; else the single active task; else (zero / more-than-one) the write rejects

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
